business.services.1.details.title: Choosing the right structure
business.services.1.details.items.0.a: A eenmanszaak is faster, cheaper and taxed through income tax with entrepreneur deductions, but you are personally liable. A BV separates your liability, reads as more substantial to Dutch clients and banks, and becomes tax-efficient once profits are meaningful. Most consultants start as a eenmanszaak and convert when the numbers justify the notary.
business.services.1.details.items.1.q: How long does a BV take?
business.services.1.details.items.1.a: Usually one to three weeks. The notary needs identification, the intended structure and a name check, and the KvK registration follows the deed. Where shareholders are abroad, legalised powers of attorney add time, so we start those first.
business.services.1.details.items.2.q: Can I incorporate before I have residence?
business.services.1.details.items.2.a: You can hold shares in a Dutch company from abroad, but working in it in the Netherlands needs the right permit. Setting up the company first and thinking about residence afterwards is the sequence that causes most of the problems we repair.
business.services.1.details.items.3.a: It must be a real address where the company is genuinely reachable, and both the KvK and the banks now check this. Virtual office packages vary enormously in whether they survive that scrutiny, and we point you to providers that do.
business.services.1.faq.title: Before you incorporate
business.services.1.faq.items.0.q: Do I need to be in the Netherlands to incorporate?
business.services.1.faq.items.0.a: Not necessarily. A BV can be incorporated with a power of attorney while you are abroad, and we coordinate the legalized signatures the notary requires.
business.services.1.faq.items.1.q: BV or eenmanszaak, which should I choose?
business.services.1.faq.items.1.a: A BV limits liability and suits growth and investors; an eenmanszaak is lighter and cheaper to run. Tax and immigration factors tip the balance per case, so we advise on your numbers, not a rule of thumb.

business.services.2.explainer.title: What is KvK registration?
business.services.2.explainer.text.0: The KvK, Kamer van Koophandel, is the Dutch Chamber of Commerce, and registration in its trade register is what legally brings a business into existence in the Netherlands. Every company and every freelancer must be listed there.
business.services.2.explainer.text.1: Registration is public: your company details are visible to anyone, and clients routinely check them before contracting. The KvK passes your details to the tax authority, which is how your VAT number follows, so the activity codes you choose at registration quietly shape your tax position afterwards.

business.services.2.conditions.items.2: Non-EU nationals must show a residence permit that allows self-employment.

business.services.2.details.title: Getting the registration right
business.services.2.details.items.0.q: Why do SBI codes matter so much?
business.services.2.details.items.0.a: They describe what your company does, and banks, insurers and the tax office all read them. A code that suggests a higher-risk activity can slow or block a business bank account, and a code that is too narrow can complicate invoicing later. We choose them with you deliberately rather than picking the nearest match at the counter.
business.services.2.details.items.1.q: Can I register without a Dutch address?
business.services.2.details.items.1.a: No, and this is the most common reason a registration fails. You need an address where the business is actually reachable. We arrange compliant business addresses for clients who are still house hunting, so the company can start while the home search runs.
business.services.2.details.items.2.a: Yes. The appointment runs in Dutch, decisions are made at the desk that are hard to reverse afterwards, and having someone beside you who knows what each question means is the difference between one appointment and three.
business.services.2.details.items.3.a: You receive your KvK number the same day and your VAT number from the tax office shortly after. Then comes business banking, accounting, invoicing setup and, if relevant, the small business VAT scheme. We work through that sequence with you rather than leaving you with a certificate.
business.services.2.faq.title: KvK questions
business.services.2.faq.items.0.q: Can I register with the KvK without living in the Netherlands yet?
business.services.2.faq.items.0.a: In some cases yes, if your business genuinely operates from a Dutch address. The setup differs from a resident registration, and we assess which applies to you.
business.services.2.faq.items.1.a: The KvK charges a modest one-time registration fee, which changes periodically. We confirm the current amount when we book your appointment, and there are no hidden charges after it.
business.services.2.faq.items.2.q: Do I get my VAT number at the KvK?
business.services.2.faq.items.2.a: The KvK passes your registration to the Belastingdienst, which then issues the VAT number. We track that handover so you are not left waiting in silence, unable to invoice.

business.services.3.details.items.0.q: Why is business banking so difficult?
business.services.3.details.items.0.a: Dutch banks apply strict onboarding rules to newly incorporated companies with non-resident founders, and applications are refused for reasons that are never fully explained. What works is a clear business description, coherent SBI codes, a genuine Dutch address, evidence of intended clients and a founder who is already registered. We prepare for that rather than discovering it.
business.services.3.details.items.1.q: How do I rent without Dutch payslips?

Landlords accept entrepreneurs on the basis of business accounts, bank statements, assets, a larger deposit or a bank guarantee, and sometimes a personal guarantee from the BV. We build that file properly and present it in Dutch, which turns a refusal into a viewing.
business.services.3.details.items.2.a: The immigration assessment, always. Everything else can be reordered, but building a company on a residence basis that does not exist is unrecoverable. Once the route is confirmed, the company, the housing and the family arrangements run in parallel.

business.services.6.conditions.title: Renting without payslips
business.services.6.conditions.intro: Dutch landlords are built to read employment contracts. Everything below is about giving them something they can read instead.
business.services.6.conditions.items.0: Landlords typically want gross income of three to four times the rent, and for entrepreneurs they look for the equivalent in accounts and assets.
business.services.6.conditions.items.1: Newly incorporated companies have no track record, so the founder's personal position usually carries the file.
business.services.6.conditions.items.2: Expect requests for annual accounts, a year of bank statements, an accountant's statement, or a bank guarantee.
business.services.6.conditions.items.3: Deposits are legally capped at two months of basic rent for contracts signed since 1 July 2023, and a larger deposit cannot be demanded instead.
business.services.6.conditions.items.4: A guarantee from your BV or a personal guarantee is often accepted where documents alone are not.
business.services.6.conditions.items.5: We act for you rather than for the landlord, and we take no commission from either side.
business.services.6.details.title: Building a file that convinces
business.services.6.details.items.0.q: What if my company is brand new?
business.services.6.details.items.0.a: Then the file rests on you rather than on it. Personal savings, income from your previous country, existing client contracts, a signed statement from an accountant and a bank guarantee all work. What does not work is arriving at a viewing with an explanation instead of documents.
business.services.6.details.items.1.q: Is a bank guarantee normal here?
business.services.6.details.items.1.a: It is common and entirely respectable for entrepreneurs. Your bank blocks an amount, typically two to three months of rent, and the landlord accepts that instead of an employment history. It usually costs a modest annual fee and it opens properties that would otherwise refuse you.
business.services.6.details.items.2.q: Should I say I am self-employed?
business.services.6.details.items.2.a: Always, and early. Landlords who discover it at contract stage withdraw. Landlords who are told at the start, and shown a properly prepared file in Dutch, mostly proceed. Concealment is the single fastest way to lose a property you had already won.
business.services.6.details.items.3.q: Can I rent a home and use it as my business address?
business.services.6.details.items.3.a: Often yes, for a consultancy or a service business with no visitors, but it depends on the lease and on the municipality's zoning rules. We check both before you register the address at the KvK, because unwinding it afterwards is unpleasant.
business.services.6.faq.title: Entrepreneur housing questions
business.services.6.faq.items.0.q: Can I rent without Dutch payslips?
business.services.6.faq.items.0.a: Yes, with the right presentation. Landlords accept entrepreneurial income when it is documented convincingly, and some ask for additional deposit or prepaid rent. We negotiate those terms to something reasonable.
business.services.6.faq.items.1.q: Can I register my company at my home address?
business.services.6.faq.items.1.a: Often, if the lease permits it and the activities suit a residential setting. We check the contract and the municipality rules for your specific case before you sign.
business.services.6.faq.items.2.q: How fast can you find something?
business.services.6.faq.items.2.a: That depends on budget and area, and we will tell you honestly at intake what your criteria yield in the current market. What we never do is let you fly in without a plan for where you will sleep and register.

guides.guides.0.metaTitle: Moving to the Netherlands: The Complete Guide | E & I
guides.guides.0.metaDescription: Everything a newcomer needs in order: visas, BSN, housing, health insurance, banking and settling in. A complete relocation guide to the Netherlands.
guides.guides.0.intro.0: The Netherlands is one of the easiest countries in Europe to arrive in and one of the hardest to arrive in unprepared. English is widely spoken, institutions work well, and processes are digital. But those processes interlock: you need an address to register, a registration to get your BSN, and a BSN for almost everything else.
guides.guides.0.intro.1: This guide walks through the full sequence of a move, from the permit question months before departure to the moment your household actually runs. Follow the order and the pieces fall into place.
guides.guides.0.cardText: The full sequence of a Dutch relocation, from visa to settled household.
guides.guides.0.sections.0.heading: Start with your right to reside
guides.guides.0.sections.0.paragraphs.0: Everything depends on your nationality. EU, EEA and Swiss citizens can live and work in the Netherlands without a permit and only need to register after arrival. Everyone else needs a residence permit from the IND, the Dutch immigration service, and usually an entry visa (MVV) before travelling.
guides.guides.0.sections.0.paragraphs.1: The most common routes are the highly skilled migrant permit through a recognised sponsor employer, the partner and family reunification permits, the startup and self-employment permits, and the DAFT permit for US citizens. Each has its own conditions and income requirements, and the thresholds change every year, so check current IND figures rather than relying on older blog posts.
guides.guides.0.sections.0.paragraphs.2: Decide your route before you book flights. Application and decision times of several weeks to a few months are normal, and some steps must be completed from your home country.
guides.guides.0.sections.1.heading: The first two weeks: registration and BSN
guides.guides.0.sections.1.paragraphs.0: If you stay longer than four months, you must register at the municipality where you live. Registration gives you your BSN, the citizen service number that unlocks nearly everything: employment payroll, health insurance, banking, a phone contract, childcare and taxes.
guides.guides.0.sections.1.paragraphs.1: To register you need a residential address and your legalised personal documents, such as a birth certificate with an apostille where required. Prepare those documents before you leave your home country, because arranging them from abroad afterwards is slow and frustrating.
guides.guides.0.sections.1.bullets.0: Register at your municipality and receive your BSN
guides.guides.0.sections.1.bullets.1: Take out Dutch health insurance, mandatory within 4 months of registration
guides.guides.0.sections.1.bullets.2: Open a Dutch bank account for rent, salary and direct debits
guides.guides.0.sections.1.bullets.3: Get a Dutch SIM or number for verification codes and DigiD
guides.guides.0.sections.1.bullets.4: Apply for DigiD, your login for government and healthcare services
guides.guides.0.sections.2.heading: Housing: the hardest part of the move
guides.guides.0.sections.2.paragraphs.0: The Dutch rental market is genuinely competitive, especially in and around the big cities. Good rentals are often gone within days, viewings fill up fast, and landlords ask for proof of income and employment before they respond. Assume the housing search will take more effort than the immigration paperwork.
guides.guides.0.sections.2.paragraphs.1: Most expats rent first and consider buying later. Expect a deposit of one to two months of rent, and read any contract carefully before signing. Because your municipal registration depends on your address, securing a home where registration is allowed is not a detail, it is a requirement. Our housing guide covers the search in depth.
guides.guides.0.sections.3.heading: Work, income and the 30% ruling
guides.guides.0.sections.3.paragraphs.0: If you are employed, your employer handles payroll tax once you have a BSN. Employees recruited from abroad with specific expertise may qualify for the 30% ruling, a tax facility that leaves part of the salary untaxed for a limited number of years. The conditions and percentages have been tightened in recent years, so verify the current rules with the Belastingdienst or a tax adviser before counting on it.
guides.guides.0.sections.3.paragraphs.1: If you plan to work for yourself, you will register with the KvK, the Dutch Chamber of Commerce, and may need a specific permit depending on your nationality. Our business guide explains that route.
guides.guides.0.sections.4.heading: Settling in: from arrival to actually living here
guides.guides.0.sections.4.paragraphs.0: A move is finished when daily life runs by itself: children are in school, the GP knows your name, utilities are in your name and you know where to be on a Saturday morning. Register with a huisarts, the general practitioner who is the gateway to all Dutch healthcare, soon after arrival rather than when you first get ill.
guides.guides.0.sections.4.paragraphs.1: Give yourself a season to adjust. The Dutch are direct, agendas are sacred, and most services expect appointments. Once you learn the rhythm, the Netherlands is an exceptionally easy place to live.

guides.guides.1.title: The Dutch Immigration Process Explained
guides.guides.1.metaTitle: The Dutch Immigration Process Explained | E & I
guides.guides.1.metaDescription: How Dutch immigration actually works: IND, MVV, residence permits, sponsors, timelines and what happens after approval. Explained step by step for expats.
guides.guides.1.intro.0: Dutch immigration is orderly but layered. One agency decides on your permit, another registers you as a resident, and a third insures your healthcare. Understanding who does what, and in which order, removes most of the stress from the process.
guides.guides.1.intro.1: This guide explains the system itself: the IND, the MVV entry visa, sponsorship, the main permit types and the steps between application and a residence card in your hand.
guides.guides.1.cardText: IND, MVV, sponsors and permits: how the Dutch system actually works.
guides.guides.1.sections.0.heading: Who decides what: IND, municipality, and you
guides.guides.1.sections.0.paragraphs.0: The IND (Immigratie- en Naturalisatiedienst) is the agency that grants visas and residence permits. It decides whether you may live in the Netherlands. Your municipality then registers where you live and issues your BSN. The two are separate: an approved permit does not register you, and registration does not extend a permit.
guides.guides.1.sections.0.paragraphs.1: For many nationalities the process starts abroad with the TEV procedure, which combines the MVV, a long-stay entry visa collected at a Dutch embassy, with the residence permit application in one decision. Nationals of some countries, including the US, Canada, the UK, Japan, Australia and New Zealand, are exempt from the MVV and can apply after arriving.
guides.guides.1.sections.1.heading: Sponsored routes: work and talent
guides.guides.1.sections.1.paragraphs.0: Most work-based permits run through a sponsor. For the highly skilled migrant permit, your employer must be an IND recognised sponsor and pay at least the applicable salary threshold, which is adjusted every year, so check current IND figures. The sponsor files the application, which usually makes this the fastest route, often decided within a few weeks.
guides.guides.1.sections.1.paragraphs.1: The EU Blue Card is a parallel route for highly qualified employees with its own salary and diploma requirements, useful for those who value mobility within the EU. Recent graduates of top universities can use the orientation year permit, which allows a year of unrestricted work searching in the Netherlands.
guides.guides.1.sections.2.heading: Family routes: partners and children
guides.guides.1.sections.2.paragraphs.0: If your partner lives in the Netherlands, or moves there with a permit, you can apply for a partner visa. The sponsoring partner must have sufficient, sustainable income, and both partners must be 21 or older. Married and unmarried durable relationships both qualify, but unmarried couples must document the relationship more extensively.
guides.guides.1.sections.2.paragraphs.1: Children under 18 can accompany or join parents through family reunification. Most adult family members apply within the civic integration framework, which for some nationalities includes a basic Dutch exam abroad before the MVV is issued. Family applications live or die on documents: legalised certificates, translations and proof of relationship, prepared exactly as the IND asks.
guides.guides.1.sections.3.heading: Independent routes: startup, self-employment and DAFT
guides.guides.1.sections.3.paragraphs.0: Entrepreneurs have three doors. The startup visa gives innovative founders one year to build under the guidance of an approved facilitator. The self-employment permit uses a points system assessing the value of your business to the Dutch economy. And US citizens have the DAFT route, based on a friendship treaty, which requires a real business and a modest capital investment held in the company, around €4,500, to be confirmed against current IND figures.
guides.guides.1.sections.3.paragraphs.1: These routes involve business plans and evidence rather than an employer sponsor, so preparation quality matters more than speed of filing.
guides.guides.1.sections.4.heading: From application to residence card
guides.guides.1.sections.4.paragraphs.0: After filing, the IND confirms receipt and states a legal decision period, often 90 days for non-sponsored routes and much shorter for recognised sponsors. You may be asked for additional documents; respond fully and on time, because incomplete files are the most common cause of delay.
guides.guides.1.sections.4.paragraphs.1: Once approved, MVV holders collect the visa at the embassy, travel, and then complete Dutch formalities in a fixed order: biometrics if not yet given, collecting the residence card at an IND desk, municipal registration for the BSN, and health insurance within four months. In some cases a TB test is also required.

guides.guides.2.title: Housing Guide for Expats in the Netherlands
guides.guides.2.metaTitle: Housing Guide for Expats in the Netherlands | E & I
guides.guides.2.metaDescription: How to find a rental home in the competitive Dutch market: where to search, what landlords require, contracts, deposits and avoiding scams.
guides.guides.2.intro.0: Ask any expat what the hardest part of their Dutch move was and most will say the same thing: finding a home. Demand outstrips supply in nearly every city, good listings disappear within days, and landlords can afford to be selective.
guides.guides.2.intro.1: The market is competitive but not impossible. Expats with the right documents ready, a realistic budget and fast follow-up find homes every week. This guide explains how the market works and how to be the candidate a landlord says yes to.
guides.guides.2.cardText: How to win a rental in the Netherlands: documents, tactics, contracts.
guides.guides.2.sections.0.heading: Understand the market you are entering
guides.guides.2.sections.0.paragraphs.0: Dutch rentals split into social housing, which has income limits and waiting lists measured in years and is effectively closed to newcomers, and the free sector, where expats rent. Free sector prices vary sharply by city and neighbourhood; Rotterdam remains more affordable than Amsterdam for comparable space, which is one reason so many internationals choose it.
guides.guides.2.sections.0.paragraphs.1: Speed defines this market. Listings appear on portals and agency sites, viewings are scheduled within days, and decisions follow quickly. Treat the search as a project with daily attention, not a weekend activity.
guides.guides.2.sections.1.heading: Prepare your file before you search
guides.guides.2.sections.1.paragraphs.0: Landlords choose the candidate whose file is complete. Before your first viewing, assemble everything a landlord or agency will ask for, in English or Dutch, as PDFs you can send within the hour.
guides.guides.2.sections.1.paragraphs.1: Income is the deciding factor. Most landlords want gross income of roughly three to four times the monthly rent, shown through an employment contract and payslips. If you are new to a job or self-employed, compensate with an employer statement, savings evidence or a longer commitment.
guides.guides.2.sections.1.bullets.2: Recent payslips, or business figures if self-employed
guides.guides.2.sections.1.bullets.3: Brief personal introduction: who you are, why you are moving
guides.guides.2.sections.1.bullets.4: References from previous landlords if you have them
guides.guides.2.sections.2.heading: Viewings and making an offer
guides.guides.2.sections.2.paragraphs.0: Respond to new listings the same day and accept the first viewing slot offered. At the viewing, check the practical things: water pressure, mould, noise, storage, and whether the property allows municipal registration. Registration is non-negotiable, because without it you cannot get your BSN at that address.
guides.guides.2.sections.2.paragraphs.1: If you want the home, say so on the spot and confirm in writing immediately after, with your file attached. In a competitive market a complete, same-day application beats a higher offer that arrives two days later.
guides.guides.2.sections.3.heading: Contracts, deposits and your rights
guides.guides.2.sections.3.paragraphs.0: Dutch law protects tenants relatively well, but you must sign a sound contract to benefit from it. Check the duration and notice period, what is included in the service costs, and how the deposit, typically one to two months of rent, is documented and returned. An inspection report with photos at check-in prevents deposit disputes at check-out.
guides.guides.2.sections.3.paragraphs.1: Rent increases, maintenance duties and service cost settlements are all regulated. If a clause looks unusual, have the contract reviewed before signing rather than contesting it afterwards. E & I reviews rental contracts for clients as a standalone service.
guides.guides.2.sections.4.heading: Avoiding scams
guides.guides.2.sections.4.paragraphs.0: Housing scarcity attracts fraud, and expats abroad are the preferred target. The pattern is always the same: an attractive price, a landlord who is conveniently overseas, and a request to transfer the deposit before you have seen the property or signed anything verifiable.
guides.guides.2.sections.4.paragraphs.1: Never pay before a viewing by you or someone you trust, verify the landlord actually owns the property, and be suspicious of any deal that is clearly below market rate. If it feels too good for this market, it is.

guides.guides.3.title: The Cost of Relocating to the Netherlands
guides.guides.3.metaTitle: The Cost of Relocating to the Netherlands | E & I
guides.guides.3.metaDescription: What a move to the Netherlands really costs: visa fees, shipping, housing deposits, insurance and monthly living costs, with honest indicative ranges.
guides.guides.3.intro.0: Every relocation budget has two layers: the one-time cost of the move itself and the recurring cost of Dutch life once you arrive. Most surprises come from the first layer, because deposits, fees and shipping all fall due in the same few weeks.
guides.guides.3.intro.1: The figures below are honest indicative ranges, not quotes. Exact amounts depend on your family size, origin country and choices, and government fees change yearly, so treat this as a planning tool and verify current figures where noted.
guides.guides.3.cardText: Honest indicative ranges for the move itself and your first Dutch months.
guides.guides.3.sections.0.heading: Immigration and document costs
guides.guides.3.sections.0.paragraphs.0: Every residence permit application carries an IND fee, typically a few hundred euros per person; the exact amounts are adjusted regularly, so check current IND figures for your permit type. Add the cost of legalising and translating documents such as birth and marriage certificates, which can run from tens to a few hundred euros per document depending on your home country.
guides.guides.3.sections.0.paragraphs.1: If your route needs professional support, a business plan, or courier trips to an embassy, budget for those as well. These costs are small next to housing, but they arrive first.
guides.guides.3.sections.1.heading: Getting yourself and your belongings here
guides.guides.3.sections.1.paragraphs.0: Flights are the predictable part. Shipping is not: a few suitcases cost nothing extra, a small partial container from within Europe might cost a low four-figure sum, and a full household container from another continent commonly runs several thousand euros, indicatively in the €4,000–€10,000 range depending on distance, volume and season.
guides.guides.3.sections.1.paragraphs.1: Many expats deliberately move light and refurnish here, which converts an uncertain shipping bill into a controllable furniture budget. The Dutch second-hand market is excellent and delivery times for new furniture are reasonable.
guides.guides.3.sections.2.heading: Housing: the big first-month outlay
guides.guides.3.sections.2.paragraphs.0: Your first housing payment is the largest single item of the move. Plan for the first month of rent plus a deposit of one to two months, all payable before you get the keys. If you rent through some agencies or take a furnished short stay to bridge the search, add those costs on top.
guides.guides.3.sections.2.paragraphs.1: As an indication, free sector rents for expat-suitable apartments in the Rotterdam region commonly start around €1,200–€1,500 per month and rise with size and location; Amsterdam is notably higher. Temporary housing for the search period typically costs more per month than a regular rental, so a fast, well-prepared search saves real money.
guides.guides.3.sections.2.bullets.0: First month of rent, payable at contract signing
guides.guides.3.sections.2.bullets.3: Temporary housing for the search period, if needed
guides.guides.3.sections.3.heading: Insurance, utilities and getting started
guides.guides.3.sections.3.paragraphs.0: Dutch health insurance is mandatory within four months of registration and costs approximately €150 per month per adult for a basic package; children under 18 are covered free under a parent. Utilities, internet and municipal taxes together typically add a few hundred euros per month for an average household.
guides.guides.3.sections.3.paragraphs.1: Then come the small unavoidable start-up costs: an OV public transport card and balance, a Dutch SIM, liability and contents insurance, which are cheap here and worth having, and the stream of household items every new home swallows in its first weeks.
guides.guides.3.sections.4.heading: A realistic total, and what changes it
guides.guides.3.sections.4.paragraphs.0: For a single professional moving from within Europe with modest belongings, the move itself, excluding ongoing rent, often lands indicatively between €3,000 and €6,000 once fees, transport, deposit and start-up costs are counted. A family shipping a container from another continent should think in the €10,000–€20,000 range. Your own figure depends mostly on three choices: how much you ship, how long you need temporary housing, and how quickly you secure a permanent rental.
guides.guides.3.sections.4.paragraphs.1: Budget a contingency of ten to twenty percent. Relocations rarely fail on the big known costs; they strain on the small simultaneous ones.

guides.guides.4.title: Living in Rotterdam as an Expat
guides.guides.4.metaTitle: Living in Rotterdam as an Expat | E & I
guides.guides.4.metaDescription: What expat life in Rotterdam is really like: neighbourhoods, housing value, international schools, transport and the character of the city.
guides.guides.4.intro.0: Rotterdam is the Netherlands nobody expects. Rebuilt after the war, it traded canals and gables for skylines and bold architecture, and it carries itself with a working-city confidence that feels closer to New York than to Amsterdam. It is also home to the largest port in Europe and one of the most international populations in the country.
guides.guides.4.intro.1: For expats the practical case is simple: more space for your money than Amsterdam, excellent connections, English spoken everywhere, and a city that genuinely absorbs newcomers because half the city arrived from somewhere else too.
guides.guides.4.cardText: Neighbourhoods, schools, transport and the real character of the city.
guides.guides.4.sections.0.heading: The character of the city
guides.guides.4.sections.0.paragraphs.0: Rotterdam is direct, unpolished in the best way, and proud of work. It is a city of makers, port logistics, architecture firms and a fast-growing food and culture scene, from the Markthal to the galleries of the Witte de Withstraat. People will not make small talk in a queue, but they will help you without ceremony when you ask.
guides.guides.4.sections.0.paragraphs.1: With over 170 nationalities, being international here is unremarkable. You will manage entirely in English while you learn Dutch, though learning basic Dutch remains the fastest way to feel at home anywhere in this country.
guides.guides.4.sections.1.heading: Neighbourhoods expats actually choose
guides.guides.4.sections.1.paragraphs.0: The centre and Kop van Zuid suit those who want apartment living with the skyline at the door: modern towers, the Erasmus Bridge, restaurants and offices within walking distance. Katendrecht, the former harbour peninsula, mixes converted warehouses with new builds and has become one of the city’s most sought-after corners.
guides.guides.4.sections.1.paragraphs.1: Families tend to look north and east: Hillegersberg and Kralingen offer houses with gardens, lakes, parks and quick access to international schools, at prices that would be fantasy in Amsterdam. Blijdorp and the Oude Noorden give a more local, pre-war streetscape, while suburbs and satellite towns such as Capelle aan den IJssel add space and value within an easy commute.
guides.guides.4.sections.2.heading: Housing value, in context
guides.guides.4.sections.2.paragraphs.0: Rotterdam remains the most affordable of the large Dutch cities, though it is no longer cheap. For the price of a one-bedroom flat in Amsterdam you will generally find a two-bedroom apartment or more here, and family houses inside the city are a realistic goal rather than a lottery win.
guides.guides.4.sections.2.paragraphs.1: The market moves fast all the same, and the best streets are contested. Everything in our housing guide applies here: complete file, same-day responses, and certainty that the address allows registration.
guides.guides.4.sections.3.heading: Schools, healthcare and daily practicalities
guides.guides.4.sections.3.paragraphs.0: Families have real choice: international schools in and around the city, Dutch schools with newcomer classes that immerse children remarkably quickly, and bilingual options in between. Popular schools have waiting lists, so start the school search as early as the housing search.
guides.guides.4.sections.3.paragraphs.1: Healthcare follows the standard Dutch model: register with a local huisarts as your first point of contact, and your insurer covers the rest. Day to day, Rotterdam is an easy city to run a life in: supermarkets everywhere, markets like the Binnenrotte for produce, and services that largely work online in English.
guides.guides.4.sections.4.heading: Getting around and getting out
guides.guides.4.sections.4.paragraphs.0: The city runs on metro, tram and bicycle, and the cycling infrastructure is as good as anywhere in the country. The metro reaches deep into the region, including the port towns to the west, which matters if your work is in Europoort or on the Maasvlakte.
guides.guides.4.sections.4.paragraphs.1: Rotterdam Centraal puts Amsterdam and Schiphol about 25 to 40 minutes away by intercity, Antwerp under an hour by high-speed train, and Paris within roughly two and a half hours. Living in Rotterdam does not mean choosing a smaller world; it means choosing a better-priced base inside the same one.

guides.guides.5.title: Relocating to Europoort: What Expats Should Know
guides.guides.5.metaTitle: Relocating to Europoort: What Expats Should Know | E & I
guides.guides.5.metaDescription: Working in Europoort or on the Maasvlakte? Where port professionals actually live, how commuting works and how to settle in the Rotterdam port region.
guides.guides.5.intro.0: Europoort is not a town, it is an engine: a vast industrial zone between Rotterdam and the North Sea where refineries, terminals, chemical plants and offshore operations employ thousands of international professionals. Together with the Botlek and the Maasvlakte it forms the working heart of the largest port in Europe.
guides.guides.5.intro.1: Nobody lives inside Europoort, so the real relocation question is different from a city move: where do you live for the best life and the best commute. This guide answers that, from daily practice guiding port professionals and their families into the region.
guides.guides.5.cardText: The port cluster, the commute, and where port professionals really live.
guides.guides.5.sections.0.heading: Understanding the port cluster
guides.guides.5.sections.0.paragraphs.0: The port of Rotterdam stretches more than forty kilometres from the city to the sea. Europoort and the Botlek hold much of the refining, chemical and liquid bulk industry; the Maasvlakte, built into the North Sea, hosts the deep-sea container terminals, offshore wind logistics and energy infrastructure.
guides.guides.5.sections.0.paragraphs.1: Employers here range from global energy and chemical companies to terminal operators, maritime service firms and offshore contractors. Contracts are often specialised and international, which is why the region draws engineers, maritime officers, project managers and technicians from all over the world, many arriving on highly skilled migrant permits arranged by their employer.
guides.guides.5.sections.1.heading: Where port professionals actually live
guides.guides.5.sections.1.paragraphs.0: The towns on and around the Voorne-Putten island are the natural home base. Rozenburg sits directly at the gates of Europoort. Brielle offers a genuinely beautiful fortified old town minutes from the industry. Hellevoetsluis adds a historic harbour and family housing near the coast, and Spijkenisse is the largest of the group, with the most housing stock, shops and a direct metro line into Rotterdam.
guides.guides.5.sections.1.paragraphs.1: Each trades differently between commute, character and housing supply. Families often favour Brielle and Hellevoetsluis for space and schools; singles and couples weigh Spijkenisse for its stock and transit or choose Rotterdam itself for city life at the cost of a longer drive.
guides.guides.5.sections.1.bullets.0: Rozenburg: shortest commute, village scale, directly beside the port
guides.guides.5.sections.1.bullets.1: Brielle: historic fortified town, popular with families
guides.guides.5.sections.1.bullets.2: Hellevoetsluis: coastal, spacious, strong family housing
guides.guides.5.sections.1.bullets.3: Spijkenisse: most housing and amenities, metro to Rotterdam
guides.guides.5.sections.1.bullets.4: Rotterdam city: full urban life, 30–50 minutes to most port sites by car
guides.guides.5.sections.2.heading: The commute, honestly
guides.guides.5.sections.2.paragraphs.0: The port runs on cars. Sites are spread out, shifts start early, and public transport covers the residential towns far better than the industrial zones themselves, though bus lines and employer shuttles serve major sites. For most port jobs a car is not optional, so arrange your driving licence exchange early; whether your foreign licence can be exchanged depends on your country and, in some cases, on holding the 30% ruling, so check the current RDW rules.
guides.guides.5.sections.2.paragraphs.1: From the Voorne-Putten towns, most Europoort and Botlek sites are within 15 to 30 minutes by car outside peak hours; the Maasvlakte adds time simply through distance. From Rotterdam, count on 30 to 50 minutes and plan around the tunnels at rush hour.
guides.guides.5.sections.3.heading: Settling a family in the port region
guides.guides.5.sections.3.paragraphs.0: The formalities are the same as anywhere in the Netherlands: municipal registration and BSN in the town where you live, health insurance within four months, a huisarts nearby. The towns are well equipped with Dutch schools, and children of internationals settle in faster than parents expect; international school options concentrate in and around Rotterdam, reachable from the whole region.
guides.guides.5.sections.3.paragraphs.1: What the region offers in exchange for its industry is easy to miss from a job description: North Sea beaches at Rockanje and Oostvoorne, water sports on the Brielse Meer, and quiet green towns where housing costs noticeably less than in the city. Many families who came for a contract stay for the life.
guides.guides.5.sections.4.heading: Why local guidance matters more here
guides.guides.5.sections.4.paragraphs.0: Big-city relocation agencies rarely know this region; their networks stop at the Rotterdam ring road. But the practical questions of a port relocation are local ones: which street in Rozenburg suits shift work, which Brielle landlords accept expat contracts, how to time a municipality appointment in Nissewaard.

guides.guides.6.title: Starting a Business in the Netherlands: A Guide
guides.guides.6.metaTitle: Starting a Business in the Netherlands: A Guide | E & I
guides.guides.6.metaDescription: How internationals start a business in the Netherlands: residence routes, KvK registration, legal forms, taxes and banking, explained step by step.
guides.guides.6.intro.0: The Netherlands is one of the most attractive places in Europe to start a business as an international: an open economy, English-friendly institutions, a strategic location around the port of Rotterdam and Schiphol, and a company registration process that takes days rather than months.
guides.guides.6.intro.1: For a non-Dutch founder the work splits into two tracks that must line up: your personal right to reside and work here, and the business formalities themselves. This guide walks through both in the order they actually happen.
guides.guides.6.cardText: Residence routes, KvK, legal forms and taxes for international founders.
guides.guides.6.sections.0.heading: First track: your right to run a business here
guides.guides.6.sections.0.paragraphs.0: EU, EEA and Swiss citizens can start a business in the Netherlands without any permit. Everyone else needs a residence status that allows self-employment, and choosing the right route is the single most important decision of the whole process.
guides.guides.6.sections.0.paragraphs.1: The startup visa suits innovative founders: one year of residence to develop the concept under an approved facilitator, with a path to the self-employment permit afterwards. The regular self-employment permit assesses your plan on a points system covering experience, financing and value to the Dutch economy. US citizens have the most accessible route of all in the DAFT permit, which requires a genuine business and an investment held in the company of around €4,500, to be confirmed against current IND figures. Holders of some other permits, such as partner permits, may already have full work rights, so check what your status allows before assuming you need a new one.
guides.guides.6.sections.1.heading: Choosing a legal form
guides.guides.6.sections.1.paragraphs.0: Most founders choose between two forms. The eenmanszaak, a sole proprietorship, is fast and cheap to set up and administratively light, but you are personally liable for business debts. The besloten vennootschap, or BV, is a private limited company: it separates business liability from your personal assets, is expected by many corporate clients and investors, and requires a notary to incorporate.
guides.guides.6.sections.1.paragraphs.1: A common pattern is to start as an eenmanszaak and convert to a BV once revenue, risk or investors justify it. If you expect significant liability or outside investment from day one, start with the BV.
guides.guides.6.sections.2.heading: Registering with the KvK
guides.guides.6.sections.2.paragraphs.0: Every business must register with the KvK, the Dutch Chamber of Commerce. You book an appointment, prove your identity and business address, describe your activities and pay a modest one-time registration fee; check the current amount on kvk.nl. You leave with a KvK number, and the KvK passes your details to the tax office automatically, which issues your VAT identification where applicable.
guides.guides.6.sections.2.paragraphs.1: You will need a Dutch business address and, for the process around it, your BSN, which is one reason the residence and registration steps must precede the business ones. A BV additionally requires a notarial deed of incorporation before the KvK registration is completed.

guides.guides.6.sections.3.heading: Taxes, banking and administration
guides.guides.6.sections.3.paragraphs.0: Dutch business taxation is manageable but unforgiving of neglect. Sole proprietors pay income tax on profits and may qualify for entrepreneur deductions if they meet the hours criterion; BVs pay corporate tax and directors pay themselves a salary under specific rules. Most businesses file VAT returns quarterly. Rates, brackets and deductions change yearly, so engage a bookkeeper or accountant from the start; for most founders it is the best money the business spends.
guides.guides.6.sections.3.paragraphs.1: Open a dedicated business bank account early. Dutch and fintech banks both serve non-Dutch founders, but onboarding checks can take weeks for newcomers, so start this in parallel with your KvK registration rather than after it.
guides.guides.6.sections.4.heading: The founder’s life around the business
guides.guides.6.sections.4.paragraphs.0: A business does not relocate, a person does. Alongside the company you will still need everything any expat needs: housing that allows registration, health insurance within four months, possibly schools, and a home base that fits the life you are building. Founders consistently underestimate how much this personal layer competes with the business for attention in the first months.
